analysis.one_liner: Restricts how pharmacy middlemen called PBMs can make money in Medicare and bans hidden markups in Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Finance Committee in December 2023 but never received a Senate vote, dying when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are companies that insurance plans hire to negotiate drug prices and decide which pharmacies patients can use. This bill would stop PBMs from making money off markups and price spreads in Medicare and Medicaid, force them to disclose what they earn on every drug, and ban them from steering prescriptions to pharmacies they own. It passed out of the Senate Finance Committee but never got a vote on the Senate floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, who would see drug pricing fees and rebates disclosed and passed through rather than kept as PBM profit; and independent pharmacies, which would be paid the full dispensed amount under Medicaid and judged by fair, standardized performance measures instead of PBM-set penalty systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and independent pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Bars PBMs in Medicare from earning anything beyond flat, fair-market service fees, and lets manufacturers' rebates count only if they are fully passed through to plans to lower drug costs.

Outlaws Medicaid spread pricing: PBMs must pass through the full ingredient cost and dispensing fee to pharmacies and may keep only a fair-market administrative fee, with all costs disclosed to the state.

Requires PBMs to report to plans and the government what they earn on every drug, what share of prescriptions their own affiliated pharmacies fill, and why brand drugs are favored over cheaper generics and biosimilars; sponsors get audit rights to verify it.

Requires plans to disclose all fees and price concessions to pharmacies at the time of payment, and replaces PBM-designed pharmacy performance penalties with standardized, evidence-based measures so independent pharmacies are not unfairly graded.

Restricts plans from limiting which network pharmacies may dispense a drug unless the drug truly requires special handling, and orders studies of PBM mark-ups, drug shortages, and price-based fees across the drug supply chain.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their insurance-company parents, which would lose spread-pricing revenue, price-based fees, and the ability to steer business to affiliated pharmacies; plans would face new reporting and audit obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBM companies and insurers that own them

drawbacks.text: Compliance burden: PBMs and plan sponsors would face extensive annual reporting, audit obligations, and standardized formats, and the bill appropriated roughly $31 million to administser it; some of that cost could flow into premiums or plan administrative fees.

The bill covers only Medicare Part D and Medicaid, not the much larger commercial insurance market where PBMs do most of their business, and much of the information it collects is shielded from public release, leaving enforcement dependent on federal agencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback is compliance cost: sweeping annual reporting, audits, and standardized performance measures would fall on PBMs and plan sponsors, and some of that cost could ultimately appear in premiums or administrative fees; the confidentiality rules also keep most reported pricing data out of public view. But the bill targeted only the Medicare and Medicaid slices of the PBMs' business, leaving the commercial insurance market untouched, and its transparency measures relied on regulators to act on what was reported. Weighed against the documented spread-pricing and self-dealing problems it addressed, the bill was a serious, if partial, attempt at accountability whose cost to the public was that it never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee approved it in December 2023 and put it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never took it up before the Congress ended, so it died.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced S. 2973 on September 28, 2023, and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which he chairs.

On December 7, 2023, the Finance Committee reported the bill with an amendment and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 266) — the waiting list for a floor vote.
The Senate never voted on the bill, no further action was taken after December 7, 2023, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.
The bill had no cosponsors listed, so it never accumulated the visible bipartisan support that helps bills reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them, who keep their current pricing practices untouched in federal programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM middlemen and insurers who own them

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: Chair, Senate Finance Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and reported it out of the Finance Committee with an amendment on December 7, 2023.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably with a written report (No. 118-122) and placed it on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no listed cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill would strip PBMs of spread pricing in Medicaid, price-based fees in Medicare, and much of their rebate-retention and self-preferencing business, while exposing their margins to government and plan-sponsor review. It does not ban PBMs, but it attacks the pricing structures at the center of their profits.

Pharmacies would keep the full dispensed amount under Medicaid pass-through pricing instead of having it clawed back, face fairer standardized performance measures, and gain protection from plans steering prescriptions to PBM-owned pharmacies.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers with PBM and pharmacy arms (e.g., CVS/Aetna, Cigna/Express Scripts, UnitedHealth/Optum)
industries.note: These companies would face the strictest disclosure about steering patients to affiliated pharmacies and internal mark-ups, though they could keep the PBM role itself as the plan's negotiating agent under the new fee rules.

Manufacturers would face disclosure of rebate contracts that tie one drug's placement to another's, and scrutiny of biosimilar and generic access, but the bill leaves manufacturer pricing itself untouched.
